title: Commission fines Google €890 million for breaches of the Digital Markets Act
bib_title: Commission fines Google for breaches of the Digital Markets Act
key_claim: On 23 July 2026 the Commission adopted two non-compliance decisions against Google, fining it 460 million euros for self-preferencing its own services in Google Search and 430 million euros for restricting app developers from steering users to alternative offers, and ordered Google to bring the non-compliance to an end.
frame_summary: Argues that the DMA's ranking and steering obligations are being applied as written, with the order to end the conduct, not the fine, as the operative instrument.
signals_supported: EU platform fines and remedies land
cluster: Orders, duties and clocks set the pace
verbatim_quote: In this regard, the Commission issued Google a fine of €460 million and a fine of €430 million respectively.
verbatim_list: Commission fines Google €890 million for breaches of the Digital Markets Act

The Commission found that Google gives preferential treatment to its own services, including shopping, hotels, transport and sports results, over those of third parties in Google Search, thereby breaching its obligations under the DMA.
As part of today's two decisions, the Commission has ordered Google to bring the non-compliance to an end.

title: EU Fines Google €890 Million Under DMA, Orders Search Redesign in 60 Days
bib_title: EU fines Google under the DMA and orders a search redesign in 60 days
key_claim: The decision carries a 60-day compliance deadline falling on 21 September 2026, after which the Commission can impose periodic penalty payments of up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover, and an appeal would not suspend that deadline.
frame_summary: Argues the decision is the first real test of whether DMA remedies change gatekeeper behaviour, since the compliance clock runs whether or not Google appeals.
signals_supported: EU platform fines and remedies land
cluster: Orders, duties and clocks set the pace
verbatim_quote: The penalty is Google's first under the DMA, dwarfs every prior sanction under that regulation, and attaches a 60-day compliance deadline that could trigger additional daily penalties if not met.

title: Commission fines Temu €200 million for breaching the Digital Services Act
bib_title: Commission fines Temu for breaching the Digital Services Act
key_claim: The Commission fined Temu 200 million euros on 28 May 2026 for failing to assess the systemic risk of illegal products reaching EU consumers, citing mystery shopping in which a very high percentage of selected chargers failed basic safety tests.
frame_summary: Argues that the DSA's risk-assessment duty is enforceable in its own right, and that a marketplace answers for the goods its design puts in front of consumers.
signals_supported: EU platform fines and remedies land

verbatim_list: The company failed to diligently identify, analyse, and assess the systemic risks of illegal products being offered on its platform and the resulting harm to consumers in the European Union.

title: Progress at the Expense of Accountability: Why the European Commission's Approach to DMA Compromise Falls Short
bib_title: Why the Commission's approach to DMA compromise falls short
key_claim: The Commission settled its Meta pay-or-consent and Apple distribution and steering cases through negotiated compromises without a published reasoned decision, leaving the substance of compliance untested judicially and publicly.
frame_summary: Argues DMA enforcement is falling short because the Commission prefers closed-door agreements with gatekeepers over contestable decisions, which forecloses third-party redress.
signals_supported: EU platform fines and remedies land
cluster: Orders, duties and clocks set the pace
verbatim_quote: In sum, the enforcer signals a clear predilection for behind-closed-doors agreements with gatekeepers to steer clear of accountability, both judicially and socially.

title: The Revised EU Product Liability Directive: State of Play Across EU Member States and Evolving Risk Landscape
bib_title: The revised EU Product Liability Directive: state of play across member states
key_claim: Ahead of the 9 December 2026 transposition deadline for Directive (EU) 2024/2853, draft transposition bills had been published in ten member states and only Hungary had adopted its implementing law, with national drafts already diverging on evidence disclosure and the development-risk defence.
frame_summary: Argues that a maximum-harmonisation directive is producing divergent national regimes, so the practical exposure for software and AI-enabled products is unpredictable rather than uniform.
signals_supported: Software and AI enter strict product liability
cluster: Orders, duties and clocks set the pace
verbatim_quote: The EU PLD represents a fundamental shift in Europe's product liability regime, particularly with regard to perceived gaps in the areas of digital products, software, and AI-driven technologies.

title: Commission's 2025 Safety Gate Report shows increased action against dangerous products and stronger consumer protection
bib_title: Safety Gate report for 2025: alerts and national follow-up actions
key_claim: In 2025 the Safety Gate system carried 4,671 alerts, the highest number since it launched in 2003 and 13% more than in 2024, alongside a record 5,794 national follow-up actions.
frame_summary: Argues that the modernised product-safety regime is working, presenting record alert and follow-up volumes as evidence of enforcement capacity rather than of a worsening safety problem.

verbatim_quote: In 2025, 4,671 alerts were notified in the Safety Gate system, the highest recorded number since the system was launched in 2003.

title: IEEPA Tariff Refunds Update: Good Progress, but Still a Ways to Go
bib_title: Tariff refunds after the IEEPA ruling: progress and friction
key_claim: As of 29 June 2026, more than four months after the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, US Customs and Border Protection had authorised $104.29 billion in refunds and paid out $71.06 billion including interest, with roughly $100.65 billion still owed.
frame_summary: Argues that the refund machinery is working but its friction falls hardest on smaller importers, so a court victory does not translate cleanly into money returned.
signals_supported: Court-ordered tariff refunds reset trade compliance
cluster: Orders, duties and clocks set the pace
verbatim_quote: CBP has authorized $104.29 billion in refunds and paid out $71.06 billion
verbatim_list: As of June 29 (more than four months after the ruling), CBP has authorized $104.29 billion in refunds and paid out $71.06 billion (including interest).
Indeed, that only $71.06 billion of the approved $104.29 billion has actually been paid suggests that frictions built into the CAPE process are creating obstacles for importers seeking refunds.

title: Commission starts enforcing AI Act rules and new transparency requirements on 2 August
bib_title: Commission starts enforcing AI Act rules and new transparency requirements from 2 August
key_claim: From 2 August 2026 the AI Office and national authorities began enforcing the AI Act, including transparency duties requiring chatbots to disclose that they are AI and AI-generated content to be marked.
frame_summary: Argues that the AI Act's enforcement phase has begun in earnest, presenting supervision and transparency duties as practical compliance routes rather than as a burden.
signals_supported: EU AI Act enforcement switches on
cluster: Orders, duties and clocks set the pace
verbatim_quote: From 2 August 2026, the European Commission’s AI Office, together with national authorities, will begin enforcing the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Act.

title: European Commission Publishes Delegated Act on Revised ESRS and Voluntary Sustainability Reporting Standard
bib_title: Delegated act on the revised ESRS and a voluntary reporting standard

key_claim: The Commission adopted and published the delegated act carrying the revised ESRS together with a voluntary reporting standard on 3 July 2026, and both acts went to the European Parliament and Council for scrutiny.
frame_summary: Argues the simplification of European sustainability reporting is now a finished piece of law-making whose remaining steps are procedural scrutiny and first application.

title: EU Pay Transparency Directive: The Deadline for Transposition Has Passed, What Now?
bib_title: EU Pay Transparency Directive: the transposition deadline has passed
key_claim: As of 5 June 2026 only Italy, Slovakia, Lithuania and Malta had implemented the Pay Transparency Directive with an effective date of 7 June 2026, while the Netherlands, Sweden, Czech Republic and Denmark had confirmed delayed implementation to 1 January 2027.
frame_summary: Argues that fragmented transposition does not buy employers time, because national courts are increasingly likely to read existing equal-pay law in line with the directive before local implementation arrives.
signals_supported: Pay transparency deadline passes unmet
cluster: The clock moves to national capitals
verbatim_quote: On 7 June 2026, the deadline for EU member states to transpose the Pay Transparency Directive (the Directive) passed.
verbatim_list: Countries that have implemented the Directive with an effective date of 7 June 2026: Italy, Slovakia, Lithuania, Malta (which we understand published legislation on the evening of 5 June 2026, and at the time of publishing we understand the regulations to be in force).
However, it is possible and increasingly likely that local courts could interpret existing national legislation in accordance with certain provisions of the Directive.

title: EU Pay Transparency Directive 2026: no EU-level delay and no time for employers to wait
bib_title: EU Pay Transparency Directive: no EU-level delay on offer
key_claim: The European Commission has confirmed there will be no pause, extension or carve-out for the Pay Transparency Directive through a future simplification package, even though most member states missed the 7 June 2026 deadline and several have not begun a formal legislative process.
frame_summary: Argues that the simplification agenda stops at the door of employment law, so the missed deadline turns pay transparency from a future project into a live compliance problem.
signals_supported: Pay transparency deadline passes unmet
cluster: The clock moves to national capitals
verbatim_quote: The 7 June 2026 transposition deadline has passed, and the European Commission has made clear that there will be no pause, no extension and no carve-out through a future simplification package.

title: Keine rechtzeitige Umsetzung der EU-Entgelttransparenzrichtlinie in deutsches Recht, was gilt nach dem 7. Juni 2026?
bib_title: Keine rechtzeitige Umsetzung der EU-Entgelttransparenzrichtlinie in deutsches Recht
date_evidence: News 03.06.2026 Am 7. Juni 2026 läuft die Frist zur Umsetzung der EU-Entgelttransparenzrichtlinie
key_claim: Germany will miss the 7 June 2026 transposition deadline for the Entgelttransparenzrichtlinie, with the implementing law expected to enter into force in early 2027, while Article 157 TFEU and directive-consistent interpretation already shape what employers must do from 8 June 2026.
frame_summary: Argues that a missed national deadline creates no legal vacuum, because courts will read existing German law in line with the directive, so employers cannot treat the delay as breathing space.
signals_supported: Pay transparency deadline passes unmet
cluster: The clock moves to national capitals
verbatim_quote: Am 7. Juni 2026 läuft die Frist zur Umsetzung der EU-Entgelttransparenzrichtlinie (RL (EU) 2023/970, im Folgenden: ETRL) in deutsches Recht ab.
verbatim_list: Ab dem 8. Juni 2026 entfaltet die ETRL über das Primärrecht und die Pflicht zur richtlinienkonformen Auslegung unmittelbare Wirkung auf das deutsche Arbeitsrecht.
Nach neuesten Meldungen aus dem zuständigen Bundesfamilienministerium soll das Gesetz Anfang 2027 in Kraft treten, wobei einige zentrale Auflagen noch nicht ab dem Inkrafttreten gelten sollen.

title: EU Platform Work Directive: which countries have implemented?

title: App group accuses Apple, Google of noncompliance with Japan smartphone law

key_claim: On 21 August 2026 the Coalition for App Fairness wrote to the Japan Fair Trade Commission arguing that Apple's and Google's July compliance reports under the Mobile Software Competition Act show unwillingness to give up rent extraction, and asked the regulator to take formal enforcement action.
frame_summary: Argues that Japan risks becoming the weak link among the new platform regimes unless its regulator moves from compliance reporting to enforcement.

title: Apple and Japan's Smartphone Act: A Compliance Report and a Fairness Complaint

key_claim: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules bring the consent manager framework into force on 13 November 2026, with the substantive notice, consent, security and breach-reporting obligations commencing on 13 May 2027.
frame_summary: Argues that the real Indian compliance work falls in 2026, because the consent architecture has to be built and tested before the substantive duties and penalties arrive.
